<img src="../man/figures/CAIBI.png" align="right" alt="" width="120"/>

This vignette walks through a full RNA-seq analysis with `CAIBIrnaseq`, from a
raw count matrix to a set of figures you could put in a report. It combines
what used to be two separate notebooks (supervised and unsupervised analysis)
into one narrative, because in practice you rarely run one without the other:
knowing *how* samples differ (unsupervised) and *why* they differ, in terms of
a comparison you care about (supervised), are two views of the same dataset.

At each step we explain **what the step does biologically**, and **what to
consider when adapting it to your own data**. Look out for callout boxes like
this one:

> **Decision point.** These call out places where the "right" choice depends
> on your experimental design, not on the package.

**R background.** This vignette assumes you can read and lightly edit R code
(change a variable, swap an argument), but doesn't assume much beyond that.
If you're new to R, [Hands-On Programming with R](https://rstudio-education.github.io/hopr/)
is a good, free place to get comfortable with the basics before diving in,
in particular its chapters on vectors, data frames, and functions cover most
of what you'll see reused below. Where we use a less common pattern (like the
`S4` objects and accessor functions Bioconductor packages rely on), we call
it out and explain it the first time it comes up.

We use the `airway` package as example data: RNA-seq of **human bronchial
epithelial cell lines**, treated or not with **dexamethasone**, a
corticosteroid expected to trigger an anti-inflammatory, stress-response
program. The treatment is recorded in the `dex` column of the sample metadata.

```{r dependencies}
#| message: false
library(airway)
library(SummarizedExperiment)
# library(CAIBIrnaseq)
devtools::load_all()
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
```

As you go through the notebook, you'll define a handful of variables right
before the step that uses them (gene/pathway names, grouping variables,
number of clusters, etc.), so you can adapt each one to your own dataset
without hunting through the surrounding code.

## Load data

All the functions below expect a `SummarizedExperiment` object as input. If
you're not familiar with this class, see the
[Bioconductor documentation](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/SummarizedExperiment/inst/doc/SummarizedExperiment.html).

If your data was generated by CAIBI from an nf-core/RNAseq pipeline, the
`salmon.merged.gene_counts_scaled.rds` object included with the outputs is
already in the right shape. Otherwise, you'll need to build one yourself and
attach gene annotation metadata (you can use `biomaRt::getBM`, shown below as
an optional chunk).

```{r load_data}
#| message: false
data(airway, package = "airway")
exp_data <- airway
rowData(exp_data)$gene_length_kb <-
  (rowData(exp_data)$gene_seq_end - rowData(exp_data)$gene_seq_start) / 1000

# If you are using your own dataset (.RDS file), use this instead:
# exp_data <- readRDS(data_file)
exp_data
```

`CAIBIrnaseq` functions expect `rowData` to contain a few standard columns.
Datasets are rarely annotated identically, so you may need to rename or
derive them:

- **gene_name**: the commonly used gene symbol (e.g. `A1BG`)
- **gene_id**: a stable identifier, typically Ensembl, sometimes ENTREZ ID for older datasets
- **gene_length_kb**: gene length in kilobases
- **gene_biotype**: `protein_coding`, `lncRNA`, `pseudogene`, etc.
- **gene_description** *(optional)*: a short functional description

```{r}
#| message: false
#| eval: false
# Only needed if your rowData doesn't already have these columns.
library(biomaRt)

mart <- useEnsembl("ensembl", dataset = "hsapiens_gene_ensembl")
gene_ids <- rowData(exp_data)$gene_id

annot <- getBM(
  attributes = c("ensembl_gene_id", "gene_name", "description"),
  filters = "ensembl_gene_id",
  values = gene_ids,
  mart = mart
)

matched <- match(rowData(exp_data)$gene_id, annot$ensembl_gene_id)
rowData(exp_data)$gene_description <- annot$description[matched]
```

## Pre-processing

### Rename to gene symbols

Aligners typically report Ensembl gene IDs. `rebase_gexp` renames features to
gene symbols (falling back to the Ensembl ID when a symbol is missing or
duplicated), so that genes are easy to refer to in the rest of the analysis.
Skip this step if `exp_data` already uses gene symbols as row names.

```{r}
#| message: false
exp_data <- rebase_gexp(exp_data, keep_cols = c(
  "gene_name", "gene_id",
  "gene_biotype", "gene_length_kb"
))
exp_data
```

### Filter low-count genes

Genes with very low or sporadic counts add noise without adding power, and
can destabilize the variance estimates used downstream. `filter_gexp` removes
them before normalization.

> **Decision point.** `min_counts` and `min_nsamp` control how aggressive the
> filter is. The defaults below (`min_counts = 1`, `min_nsamp = 1`) only drop
> genes with zero expression everywhere, which is a safe, permissive default
> for most analyses. If you have many samples per group and want to focus on
> genes with a reasonable chance of being detected reliably, consider raising
> `min_nsamp` to something close to your smallest group size.

```{r}
#| message: false
exp_data <- filter_gexp(exp_data, min_nsamp = 1, min_counts = 1)
```

Check that the filter behaves sensibly on your data before moving on — you
want to remove the low-count tail without cutting into genes you actually
care about:

```{r plot_qc_filters}
#| warning: false
#| message: false
colData(exp_data)$sample_id <- colnames(exp_data)
plot_qc_filters(exp_data)
```

### Normalize

Raw counts aren't directly comparable between samples because of differences
in sequencing depth and composition. `normalize_gexp` handles this
automatically: it uses `DESeq2::rlog` for small sample sizes and switches to
the faster `DESeq2::vst` once you have enough samples for it to behave well.
Both stabilize the variance across the expression range, which is what makes
PCA, clustering, and heatmaps meaningful.

```{r}
#| message: false
exp_data <- normalize_gexp(exp_data)
```

## Explore the samples (unsupervised)

Before testing any specific hypothesis, it's worth looking at how samples
relate to each other with no prior assumptions about grouping. This tells you
whether the structure you expect (e.g. treatment groups) is actually the
dominant source of variation, or whether something else (batch, sex, sample
quality) is competing with it.

We define the grouping variable we ultimately care about here, which is the column in `colData` for our condition of interest, and reuse it throughout the
rest of the vignette to color and annotate plots.

```{r}
#| message: false
group_var <- "dex" # column in colData with your condition of interest

metadata(exp_data)[["pca_res"]] <- pca_gexp(exp_data)
pca_plot <- plot_pca(exp_data, color = group_var, ellipses = TRUE, out = "ggplot")
pca_plot
```

**A note on `metadata()`.** `exp_data` is a `SummarizedExperiment`, an `S4`
object (a more structured kind of R object than the lists and data frames you
may be used to, common in Bioconductor packages). You don't interact with its
internal slots directly; instead you use accessor functions like `assay()`,
`colData()`, `rowData()`, and `metadata()` to read and write specific parts
of it. `metadata()` gives you a general-purpose, named-list slot for
anything that doesn't fit the "one value per gene" (`rowData`) or "one value
per sample" (`colData`) shape, such as the whole `pca_res` object above.
The line `metadata(exp_data)[["pca_res"]] <- pca_gexp(exp_data)` runs
`pca_gexp()` and stores its result under the name `"pca_res"` inside
`exp_data`, so that other functions (like `plot_pca()` here) can find it
later without you having to pass it around separately. You'll see this same
pattern reused throughout the vignette to attach clustering, pathway, and
microenvironment results to `exp_data`.

If the two groups separate cleanly along a principal component, that's a
good sign the treatment effect is a major source of variance. If they
overlap heavily, don't be discouraged: subtle transcriptional effects can
still be detected by differential expression, which is a more sensitive,
targeted test than PCA.

### Unsupervised clustering

Hierarchical clustering groups samples by overall expression similarity,
independent of any known label. It's useful both as a sanity check (do
replicates cluster together?) and as a discovery tool (are there subgroups
you didn't know about?).

> **Decision point.** `k` is the number of clusters to cut the dendrogram
> into. Start from what you know about the design (e.g. number of expected
> groups) and adjust based on whether the resulting clusters look
> biologically coherent. This is often an iterative choice, not a one-shot
> calculation.

```{r}
#| message: false
exp_data <- cluster_exp(exp_data, k = 2, n_pcs = 1)
```

```{r plot_hvg}
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
hvg <- highly_variable_genes(exp_data)
hvg_heatmap <- plot_exp_heatmap(exp_data,
  genes = head(hvg, 50),
  annotations = c(group_var, "exp_cluster"),
  show_rownames = TRUE,
  show_dend_row = FALSE,
  clustering_method = "complete",
  hm_color_limits = c(-2, 2),
  fontsize = 10
)
hvg_heatmap
```

You'll notice some of these highly variable genes aren't cleanly split by treatment group at all. With only a handful of samples per group, "most variable" and "most relevant to my
comparison of interest" are not the same thing: a single sample's idiosyncratic expression (technical noise, a slightly different batch, a genuinely unusual biological replicate) can easily rank among the top HVGs by raw variance alone, without reflecting the treatment effect we actually
care about. This is exactly the limitation that differential expression
analysis, which comes next, is designed around: instead of ranking genes by
overall variance, it explicitly tests each gene *against the grouping variable itself*, so a gene that only varies because of one odd sample won't look significant.

## Differential expression (supervised)

Where the previous section let the data speak for itself, differential expression analysis directly tests a hypothesis: which genes change with a condition you specify.

### Design and contrasts

The `design` argument tells the model which variables in `colData` are sources of biological (or technical) variation to account for when computing differentially expressed genes (DEGs). Here, we treat `dex` as the only source of variation:

`DEGs ~ dex`

You can build additive models with several variables (e.g. `"~ batch + dex"`), which usually gives more accurate and stringent results than running separate analyses per variable — this is worth doing whenever
you have a known covariate like batch or sex. Interaction terms are also possible but are a more advanced topic best approached with some statistical background.

Contrasts tell the model exactly what comparison to report, as a string with
three elements separated by `_vs_`: the variable name, the numerator level,
and the denominator level. For example, `dex_trt_vs_untrt` compares treated
(`trt`) to untreated (`untrt`) samples for the `dex` variable — genes with a
positive fold-change are up-regulated in `trt`.

> **Decision point.** Available contrasts are built from the factor levels of
> your design variable, with the first level as denominator by default. Set
> the level order explicitly (as below) to make sure the comparison direction
> is what you intend — an accidentally inverted contrast is a common source
> of "backwards" results. If you don't specify contrasts, all pairwise
> comparisons are returned.

```{r}
#| message: false
colData(exp_data)$dex <- factor(colData(exp_data)$dex, levels = c("untrt", "trt"))
diffexp <- diffExpAnalysis(exp_data, design = group_var, contrasts = "dex_trt_vs_untrt")
```

### Volcano plot

A volcano plot shows statistical significance (`-log10 padj`) against effect
size (`log2FoldChange`) for every gene, making it easy to spot genes that are
both strongly and reliably changed.

```{r volcano}
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
volcano_plot <- plot_exp_volcano(diffexp, nb = 20, out = "ggplot")
volcano_plot
```

The two columns that matter most are `log2FoldChange` (the effect size, on a
log2 scale) and `padj` (the p-value adjusted for multiple testing, always
prefer this over the raw p-value to control false discoveries). Fold-changes
are shrunk with `apeglm` by default, which pulls noisy estimates toward zero
without touching genes with strong, well-supported effects (see
`? DESeq2::lfcShrink` and the
[`apeglm` paper](https://academic.oup.com/bioinformatics/article/35/12/2084/5159452)).

```{r}
#| eval: false
diffexp |> slice(1:30)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
diffexp |>
  slice(1:30) |>
  kableExtra::kbl() |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling() |>
  kableExtra::scroll_box(height = "200px")
```

## Pathway analysis

Individual genes are hard to interpret in isolation. Pathway analysis summarizes differential expression at the level of gene sets — curated collections of genes known to act together — which is usually more robust
and more directly interpretable in biological terms.

Pathway collections available in MSigDB can be browsed below (use `gs_subcollection` as the name, except for Hallmark, which is `"H"`):

```{r}
#| eval: false
msigdbr::msigdbr_collections(db_species =  "HS")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
msigdbr::msigdbr_collections() |>
  kableExtra::kbl() |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling() |>
  kableExtra::scroll_box(height = "300px")
```

> **Decision point.** Picking collections is a trade-off between specificity
> and interpretability. Hallmark gene sets (`"Hallmark"`) are small, curated,
> and easy to summarize in a report. GO Biological Process (`"GO:BP"`) is
> comprehensive but has many redundant, narrowly-defined terms. KEGG
> (`"CP:KEGG_LEGACY"`) is good when you want canonical signaling/metabolic
> pathways, e.g. to follow up with `pathview`. Combine a couple that suit your
> question rather than pulling in everything at once.

```{r}
#| message: false
collections <- c("Hallmark", "GO:BP")
pathways <- get_annotation_collection(collections, species = "Homo sapiens")
```

Gene sets that are too small are hard to trust statistically; ones that are
too large are hard to interpret. Filtering by size keeps results
manageable:

```{r}
#| message: false
keep_pathways <- pathways |>
  count(pathway) |>
  dplyr::filter(n >= 30 & n <= 500) |>
  pull(pathway)
pathways <- pathways |> filter(pathway %in% keep_pathways)
```

### Two ways to score pathways from DE results

> **Decision point.** Both methods are provided because they answer slightly
> different questions:
>
> - **ORA** (`method = "ora"`) treats your significant genes (above a chosen
>   cutoff) as a set, and tests whether each pathway is over-represented in
>   that set compared to chance (Fisher's exact test). It's fast and simple,
>   but sensitive to exactly where you draw the significance cutoff.
> - **FGSEA** (`method = "fgsea"`) avoids a hard cutoff by ranking *all*
>   genes (e.g. by signed significance) and testing whether a pathway's genes
>   accumulate near the top or bottom of that ranking. It's more sensitive to
>   coordinated, subtle shifts across a pathway, at the cost of being
>   somewhat slower and less immediately intuitive to explain.
>
> If you're unsure, FGSEA is the safer general-purpose default; ORA is a good
> complement when you specifically want to reason about "my significant gene
> list".

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
pathwayResult_ora <- pathwayAnalysis(diffexp, pathways = pathways, method = "ora")
pathwayResult_fgsea <- pathwayAnalysis(diffexp, pathways = pathways, method = "fgsea")

metadata(exp_data)[["pathwayEnrichment"]] <- pathwayResult_ora
metadata(exp_data)[["pathwayEnrichment_fgsea"]] <- pathwayResult_fgsea
```

> **Decision point.** `padj_cutoff` sets how strict the significance filter is
> for the pathways shown (only used when you don't pass an explicit
> `pathways` list). The customary threshold is `padj < 0.05`; we relax it to
> `0.2` here purely so this small demo dataset (8 samples, one contrast)
> returns more than a single pathway to look at. For your own analysis,
> default back to `0.05` unless you have a specific reason to look at
> borderline hits, and treat anything you show above `0.05` as exploratory
> rather than a confirmed result.

```{r pathway_dotplot}
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
pathway_dotplot <- plot_pathway_dotplot(exp_data, score_name = "pathwayEnrichment_fgsea", padj_cutoff = 0.2)
pathway_dotplot
```

### Leading-edge genes of top pathways

FGSEA's *leading edge* for a pathway is the subset of its genes that drives the enrichment score, i.e. the genes actually pushing that pathway up (or down) the ranking. Looking at their individual expression, rather than only the pathway-level summary statistic, is a good sanity check: it tells you whether a "significant pathway" reflects a handful of strongly-changed genes, a broad coordinated shift across many genes, or something in between.

> **Decision point.** The dot plot above picks pathways automatically by
> `padj` alone, which is a reasonable default but, especially with a small
> sample size like this one, can surface hits that are statistically
> plausible but biologically incidental (e.g. a developmental or
> tissue-identity gene set with no obvious link to the treatment). For a
> figure meant to tell a specific story, it's usually better to hand-pick
> pathways that fit what you already know about the biology, then check that
> they're at least nominally supported by the data, rather than reading the
> story off an automatic ranking. Here, dexamethasone is a corticosteroid
> whose two hallmark effects are activating glucocorticoid-responsive gene
> programs directly and suppressing inflammatory signaling (classically
> NF-\U03BAB/TNF-\U03B1 target genes); we pick four pathways from the
> significant results (`padj < 0.2`, the same relaxed threshold used above)
> that reflect exactly that: direct corticosteroid/steroid-hormone response,
> the canonical xenobiotic-metabolism gene set induced through the
> glucocorticoid receptor, and repression of TNF-\U03B1/NF-\U03BAB signaling.

```{r}
#| message: false
dex_pathways <- c(
  "GOBP_RESPONSE_TO_CORTICOSTEROID",
  "GOBP_RESPONSE_TO_STEROID_HORMONE",
  "HALLMARK_XENOBIOTIC_METABOLISM",
  "HALLMARK_TNFA_SIGNALING_VIA_NFKB"
)

top_pathways <- pathwayResult_fgsea |>
  filter(pathway %in% dex_pathways, padj < 0.2) |>
  arrange(padj)

leading_edge_genes <- setNames(
  lapply(top_pathways$leadingEdge, head, 15),
  top_pathways$pathway
)
```

`leading_edge_genes` is a **named list** of gene vectors, one per pathway,
capped here at 15 genes each purely to keep the figure readable. This is a
useful pattern beyond this specific example: `plot_exp_heatmap()` (like the
other heatmap functions in this package) accepts `genes` as either a plain
character vector, or a named list like this one, in which case it draws a
**row-faceted heatmap**, one block per list element, labeled by its name.
Genes that show up in more than one pathway's leading edge are kept only in
the first group they appear in, so the row groups stay non-overlapping.

```{r leading_edge_heatmap}
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6.5
leading_edge_heatmap <- plot_exp_heatmap(exp_data,
  genes = leading_edge_genes,
  annotations = group_var,
  show_rownames = TRUE,
  show_dend_row = FALSE,
  rows_title = "Genes in leading edge",
  column_title = "Samples",
  hm_color_limits = c(-2, 2),
  group_prop = 0.02
)
leading_edge_heatmap
```

### Single-sample pathway scores

The scores above summarize the group-level comparison. It's often useful to
also compute a score *per sample*, so you can see the distribution within
each group rather than only a single summary statistic, and check for
outliers.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
pathway_scores <- score_pathways(exp_data, pathways, verbose = FALSE)
metadata(exp_data)[["pathway_scores"]] <- pathway_scores
```

We visualize this as a "beeswarm" boxplot — every sample as a point, plus the
group mean and a Wilcoxon rank-sum test:

```{r}
#| message: false
boxplot_pathways <- c(
  "GOBP RESPONSE TO CORTICOSTEROID",
  "GOBP REGULATION OF SMALL MOLECULE METABOLIC PROCESS"
)

pathway_boxplots <- lapply(boxplot_pathways, function(path) {
  plot_pathway_boxplot(exp_data,
    pathway = path,
    annotation = group_var,
    color_var = group_var,
    pt_size = 2
  )
})
```

```{r}
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.5
wrap_plots(pathway_boxplots, nrow = 1, guides = "collect")
```

## PROGENy: core signaling pathway activity

As an alternative to gene-set-based scoring, PROGENy infers activity for 14
well-characterized signaling pathways from a small, curated set of
responsive genes (see the
[original paper](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-017-02391-6)).
Because it relies on far fewer genes per pathway than MSigDB collections, it
tends to be more robust to noise but covers a narrower biological scope —
useful as a quick, complementary check rather than a replacement for the
pathway analysis above.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
progeny_scores <- score_progeny(exp_data, species = "Homo sapiens")
metadata(exp_data)[["progeny_scores"]] <- progeny_scores

plot_progeny_heatmap(exp_data, annotations = group_var, fontsize = 11)
```

## Microenvironment composition

If your samples are tissue (rather than pure cell lines or sorted cells),
`mcp_counter` estimates the relative abundance of immune and stromal cell
types from bulk expression, using (m)MCPcounter. This can help distinguish a
genuine treatment effect from a shift in tissue composition.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
mcp_scores <- mcp_counter(exp_data, species = "Homo sapiens")
metadata(exp_data)[["microenv_scores"]] <- mcp_scores

microenv_heatmap <- plot_microenv_heatmap(exp_data, annotations = group_var, fontsize = 11)
microenv_heatmap
```

## Targeted views on genes of interest

Once you have a global picture, it's often useful to zoom in on a specific,
curated gene signature — genes you already have reason to care about, from
the literature or from the analysis above.

```{r}
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3
heatmap_genes <- list(
  `Glucocorticoid response genes` = c("FKBP5", "TSC22D3", "PER1", "ZBTB16"),
  `Anti-inflammatory genes` = c("DUSP1", "SOCS1", "MT2A")
)

gene_heatmaps <- plot_exp_heatmap(exp_data,
                  genes = heatmap_genes,
                  annotations = group_var,
                  show_rownames = TRUE,
                  hm_color_limits = c(-1.5, 1.5),
                  show_dend_row = FALSE)
gene_heatmaps                  
```

## A quick note on KEGG pathway diagrams

For a chosen pathway, it can help to see exactly which genes are up- or
down-regulated in the context of the pathway diagram itself, rather than as a
list. This is what the companion
[Pathview vignette](pathview.html) demonstrates: converting `diffexp` results
into a `pathview`-compatible input and rendering a colored KEGG diagram. We
don't repeat the full walkthrough here since it needs an Entrez ID conversion
step that's easiest to follow on its own.

## Making a summary figure

For a report or presentation, you'll typically want a single multi-panel
figure rather than a notebook's worth of separate plots. We use
[`patchwork`](https://patchwork.data-imaginist.com/) here specifically for
its flexible layout system: it can be used in a grid and also allows to use
[`design` strings](https://patchwork.data-imaginist.com/articles/guides/layout.html)
let you lay panels out (and have them span multiple rows/columns).

Here, we combine the sample-level overview (PCA), the differential expression result (volcano plot), the pathway-level summary (dot plot), and the leading-edge gene heatmap into one proposed figure.

> Note: `plot_exp_heatmap()` (like the other heatmap functions in this package) doesn't return a plain `ggplot` panel: under the hood it's built with `ggheatmapper::ggheatmap()`, which stitches together the heatmap itself, its dendrograms, and annotation tracks. If you drop an object like that directly into a patchwork alongside simple ggplots, patchwork tries to align all of their internal panels together, and the mismatch can scramble where axis titles end up on the *other* plots. `patchwork::wrap_elements()` avoids this by treating the heatmap as a single opaque image block instead of something to align internally

```{r summary_figure}
#| fig-cap: "**Dexamethasone treatment of bronchial epithelial cells.** (A) Principal component analysis of normalized gene expression, colored by treatment (trt: dexamethasone-treated; untrt: untreated), with 95% confidence ellipses. (B) Volcano plot of differential expression between treated and untreated samples (Wald test, DESeq2, fold changes shrunk with apeglm); genes with padj < 0.05 and |log2FoldChange| > 1 are colored by direction, with the top 20 differentially expressed genes labeled. (C) Gene set enrichment analysis (FGSEA) against the Hallmark and GO Biological Process collections (MSigDB), showing the top pathways (padj < 0.2). (D) Row-faceted heatmap of scaled, normalized expression for the leading-edge genes (top 15 per pathway) of four pathways selected for their relevance to glucocorticoid signaling. Samples are hierarchically clustered (columns); genes are grouped by pathway (rows), colored by scaled expression."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 11

summary_figure <- wrap_elements(plot = pca_plot) + volcano_plot + pathway_dotplot + wrap_elements(full = leading_edge_heatmap) +
  plot_layout(widths = c(1,2), heights = c(1,1.8)) +
  plot_annotation(
    tag_levels = "A"
  ) &
  theme(plot.tag = element_text(face = "bold"))

summary_figure
```

Treat this as a starting point rather than a fixed template: swap in the
microenvironment heatmap, targeted gene heatmaps, or pathway boxplots
depending on which result is most central to the story you're telling, and
adjust `plot_layout()` (via a `design` string, if you need an irregular grid) to fit however many panels you end up with. Wrap any other heatmap panel the same way with `wrap_elements()`.

```{r}
#| eval: false
ggsave("results/summary_figure.pdf", summary_figure, width = 12, height = 9)
```

## Report parameters

For reproducibility, we record the computational environment used to
generate this analysis.

```{r}
sessionInfo()
```
